prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and its development into incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B049 first, which tells us about convergence but not about merit, so I restate the merit case. The arc runs from gut-hormone physiology (the incretin effect, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, GLP-1 actions on appetite and gastric emptying) to long-acting agonists with large, independently confirmed randomized-trial benefits in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and increasingly cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism is stable after decades of replication, and the clinical effect is among the largest of any recent therapeutic class. I keep Knudsen in my trio because the conversion of a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug (fatty-acid acylation for albumin binding, liraglutide, semaglutide) was itself a scientific step, not routine scale-up, and her contribution is the least disputed in the historical record. Holst (human physiology and secretion) and Drucker (receptor biology, proglucagon-derived peptides, cardiometabolic actions) anchor the physiology. A citation spanning physiology to therapy is also the one most faithful to the field's history.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution, not worthiness. Three names cannot cover Holst, Drucker, Mojsov, Knudsen and Habener, and whichever trio we choose will be attacked. My own trio omits Mojsov, whom four colleagues include for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and Habener, who is outside the credited names, and it includes an industrial scientist, which some will read as rewarding drug development over discovery. If the committee decides that the physiology and peptide identification are the Nobel-level discovery and the drugs are application, then Knudsen's slot is the weakest and Mojsov should replace her.

responses.point: Linnarsson excludes Knudsen because her work is industrial drug development, and the three-person limit forces a choice, so he prefers Holst, Drucker and Mojsov.
responses.response: I disagree in part. The prize has honoured the translation of a mechanism into a medicine when the chemistry was itself conceptually new, and acylation-based half-life extension is exactly that. The reason I hesitate over Mojsov is not her contribution, which I accept as real, but that her priority claim for the active peptide is the one most entangled with Habener's group, who are not in the credited set. A trio with an unresolved priority dispute carries more risk than one with an undisputed contributor. I concede that his reading is the more conventional one, and I would not block it if the room agrees that discovery rather than development should decide the trio.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also ranks B049 first with Mojsov, treats Knudsen as sitting on the industrial side, and ranks B044 (Feldmann and Maini, anti-TNF) second, partly because the pioneers are elderly.
responses.response: I accept the urgency argument for B044 but not the ranking. Anti-TNF shows that a cytokine is a therapeutic target, but TNF biology was established by others outside the credited pair, so it reads as a clinical proof of concept resting on prior discoveries. GLP-1 has a physiological discovery of its own, which makes it cleaner. I also think B014, which she ranks third, is a stronger second candidate. Her point that a prize which excludes the drug developer may look incomplete cuts toward including Knudsen, not away from it.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B014 second with June and Sadelain only, leaving out Rosenberg because adoptive cell therapy is a distinct contribution, and notes the unresolved credit for earlier CAR work.
responses.response: I agree that a two-name CAR-T configuration is cleaner than adding Rosenberg, and my own opening used the same pair. The Eshhar gap is the real problem: if the credited names omit the person who first described the chimeric receptor concept, a fair citation has to be worded around the engineering of costimulated CARs and clinical translation, not the receptor concept. I would keep B014 as my first alternative and as a natural second part if the committee wanted a shared prize, though the three-person cap would then squeeze B049.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics (B021) second and ranks TOR (B001) fourth, while warning that the six credited names for optogenetics cannot be resolved into three.
responses.response: I share his concern about B021 and ranked it only fifth for that reason. Whether the prize should go to the molecular discovery of channelrhodopsin or to its neuronal deployment is a real fork, and any trio excludes Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck. On TOR, I put it above optogenetics because the attribution is more tractable around Hall and the mechanism has the broader biomedical reach, but his and Linnarsson's unease about conduct questions concerning one credited individual is something I cannot assess from the evidence we have.

uncertainties: Whether Knudsen or Mojsov should hold the third place, which depends on how the committee weighs development against discovery and on the unresolved priority question with Habener's group.
Whether the early GLP-1 priority history that I recall from memory is accurate; I have not verified it independently.
Whether a shared prize pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T is feasible under the three-person cap without damaging the GLP-1 attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B049. My profile documents co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén and a shared KI setting, but none of that bears on the GLP-1 candidates, and I have no documented connection to any shortlisted candidate.
